1205.title: The sutras, closed
1205.hook: a sick layman, a jeweled net, a pointing finger, a roadside Jizo
1205.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia and Tibet keep, chant and study these sutras, and different communities give special place to different ones: the Vimalakirti among lay readers, the Flower Garland in Huayan and Kegon, the Medicine Buddha and Ksitigarbha sutras in temple devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Queen Srimala, who answered a letter with praise and then taught while the Buddha listened. Your line: the queen teaches.

A sick man on a couch, in a room that keeps growing to fit his guests. A net of jewels, each one shining with all the others. A fingertip raised toward the moon. A small stone figure by a road, wearing a red bib. Lay those four on a table and they don't look like they belong together. They came off one shelf. When this stretch of the path began, the promise was modest: the Mahayana sutras are many, and i'd open a handful, in paraphrase. Today the handful goes back on the shelf.
screen: `A SICK MAN, A NET, A FINGER, A STONE.` → `ONE SHELF.` → `THE HANDFUL GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: The sickroom. In the Vimalakirti Sutra, a layman is ill, and the Buddha's great disciples all find reasons not to visit. Manjushri goes, and the room makes space for everyone. Vimalakirti says he is sick because the world is sick. Flowers fall and stick to those who think flowers improper. A goddess swaps bodies with Sariputra to show that male and female are not fixed. And asked about non-duality, Vimalakirti answers with silence. The net and the tower. In the Flower Garland, as the Huayan school explains it, each jewel in Indra's net reflects all the others. Young Sudhana walks from teacher to teacher, a monk, a girl, a sailor, a king, and steps into Maitreya's tower, where every room holds every other. A world sits in a grain of dust. The finger and the storehouse. The Lankavatara warns that words are a finger pointing at the moon, not the moon, and speaks of a storehouse where the seeds of habit are kept. The ones who reach. The blue Medicine Buddha and his vows of healing. Ksitigarbha, who won't rest until the hells are empty, and who in Japan stands by the road as Jizo, guarding children. Avalokiteshvara, turning his hearing around. A golden statue in rags. A queen who teaches. Put together, the shelf has a shape. Again and again these books push against lines that seem fixed: lay and ordained, man and woman, sick and well, one thing and everything. And again and again, someone reaches across.
screen: `THE SICKROOM THAT GROWS.` · `THE NET AND THE TOWER.` · `THE FINGER AND THE STOREHOUSE.` · `THE ONES WHO REACH.` · then, large: `THE LIBRARY, OPENED.`

segments.voice: Let the pictures from these weeks pass slowly, like books along a shelf: the falling flowers, the silent layman, the net of jewels, the tower, the finger and the moon, the red bib on a stone, the gold in rags. Don't choose; notice which one the mind keeps coming back to. When one stays, let the others go, and rest with that one image.
The sutras. Discourses that open, thus have I heard, and set a teaching in a scene; in the Mahayana, a large library, of which this path has read a handful. Today's word.
Your line: the library, opened. Tomorrow the path turns from the shelf to the cushion. Shelf closed, for now.

1206.title: What Zen is
1206.hook: Chan in China, Seon in Korea, Thien in Vietnam, Zen in Japan: the school of meditation
1206.howItsDone: Chan, Seon, Thien and Zen communities in China, Korea, Vietnam, Japan and beyond gather to sit in meditation, usually alongside chanting, ritual and work, and many centers welcome beginners to sit with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sutras went back on the shelf: a sick layman, a net of jewels, a pointing finger, a stone by the road. Your line: the library, opened.

On a scroll in a meditation hall hangs a single character, brushed in black ink. Show it to a monk in China and she reads it Chan. In Korea, the same brushstrokes are Seon. In Vietnam, Thien. In Japan, Zen. Four countries, four sounds, one shape on the paper. In English the word has slipped into a mood: a zen garden, a zen playlist. But on that scroll it names something more particular, a whole school of Buddhism.
screen: `ONE CHARACTER IN BLACK INK.` → `FOUR WAYS TO READ IT.` → `A WHOLE SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Chan, Seon, Thien, Zen: these are not four schools that happen to sound alike. They are one Chinese word, carried into neighboring languages and said with each language's own mouth. Tradition traces the word back to the Sanskrit dhyana, meditation. So the school's name is, quite plainly, the meditation school. That name puts sitting at the center. For weeks this path has been reading sutras, and Zen communities chant sutras too. But the name points somewhere else first: not a book on the lap, a body on a cushion, someone who sits down, settles, and looks directly at their own mind. As the meditation school traveled, each land gave it a voice of its own. In the coming weeks this path will meet them: Korea's great question, carried through the day; Vietnam's joining of sitting and chanting; in Japan, a school that works with koans and a school of just sitting. They differ, sometimes, in emphasis. They share the same posture. So before the poems and the famous puzzles, before the old masters and the oxherding pictures, comes the body: how to sit, where the hands go, where the eyes rest, what to do with the breath. That's not a warm-up for Zen. As some Zen teachers put it, it is Zen.

segments.voice: On one out-breath, say quietly, Chan, and let the sound fade; on the next, Seon, then Thien, then Zen, resting in the quiet each one leaves behind. Notice that the names are different and the quiet after them is the same. Then let the words go and just sit, the way someone has sat in each of those countries.
Zen. The Japanese reading of a word that is Chan in China, Seon in Korea and Thien in Vietnam: the meditation school of Buddhism. Today's word.
Your line: four names, one practice. Under the mood the word has become, there's a cushion and someone sitting. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1207.title: Sitting posture
1207.hook: cross-legged, on a chair or a bench: a straight back, a relaxed body
1207.howItsDone: In Zen centers and monasteries, people sit zazen facing a wall or the room, on round cushions over flat mats, on kneeling benches or on chairs, and beginners are usually shown how to find their posture before anything else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one character read four ways: Chan, Seon, Thien, Zen, the meditation school. Your line: four names, one practice.

Take a quick inventory, right where you are. Is the head drifting forward toward a screen? Is one shoulder higher than the other? Is the lower back curled like a question mark into the couch? Nothing wrong with any of it. That's just how bodies settle when nobody is paying attention. Zen pays attention. Before any teaching about the mind, it starts with the body, and a very plain question: how are you sitting? Today's word: zazen.
screen: `HEAD FORWARD, SHOULDERS UNEVEN.` → `HOW ARE YOU SITTING?` → `ZEN STARTS WITH THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Zazen is Japanese for seated meditation: za, sitting, and zen, the meditation school's own word. A plain name for the school's central practice. First, the base. The classic postures are cross-legged on a firm round cushion: full lotus, each foot resting on the opposite thigh; half lotus, one foot up; or the easier Burmese way, both legs folded on the floor, one in front of the other. Some people kneel, on a cushion or a small wooden bench. Some sit on a chair, feet flat, not leaning back. Zen teachers today offer these. The point isn't the shape of the legs. It's a base stable enough that the body can stop holding itself up by effort. Then the spine. It rises straight, not stiff, more stacked than braced. Some teachers describe a thread lifting gently from the crown of the head. There's an old instruction, which this path will read in full later, from Dogen's guide to sitting: ears in line with the shoulders, nose in line with the navel. Anyone can check it. Then the pair: straight and relaxed. Straight alone turns into a soldier at attention, tight in the jaw and shoulders, and soon tired. Relaxed alone slumps back into the couch. Zazen asks for both at once: upright enough to stay awake, soft enough to stay there.
screen: `ZAZEN: SEATED MEDITATION.` · `A STABLE BASE: CUSHION, BENCH, CHAIR.` · `EARS OVER SHOULDERS, NOSE OVER NAVEL.` · `STRAIGHT AND RELAXED, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `UPRIGHT ENOUGH TO STAY AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Come to the front of whatever you're sitting on, let the base settle, and rock gently side to side and forward and back, each sway smaller, until you stop in the middle. Ears over shoulders, nose over navel; then let the shoulders drop and the belly soften. Straight and relaxed, simply sit there in that shape.
Zazen. Japanese for seated meditation, the central practice of Zen: a stable base, a straight back, a relaxed body. Today's word.

1208.title: The hands
1208.hook: the cosmic mudra: left hand on right, thumbs lightly touching, an oval at the navel
1208.howItsDone: In Zen sitting, practitioners usually hold the hands in the cosmic mudra for the whole period, and teachers check beginners' hands along with their posture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, zazen: a stable base, ears over shoulders, nose over navel. Your line: straight and relaxed.

Hands are hardly ever off duty. Since waking they've probably held a phone, a cup, a door handle, a spoon; typed, scrolled, pointed, waved. Even resting, they fidget. Sit down to meditate and they get restless: on the knees, then the thighs, then folded, then back on the knees. Zen gives them a job, a very small one, done resting in the lap.
screen: `HANDS ARE NEVER OFF DUTY.` → `EVEN RESTING, THEY FIDGET.` → `ZEN GIVES THEM A JOB.`

segments.voice: In zazen the hands rest in the lap in what's often called the cosmic mudra. A mudra is a gesture held with the hands, sometimes called a seal. The back of one hand rests in the palm of the other, fingers overlapping, the left on the right in the usual Soto Zen instruction. Dogen's guide to sitting gives it that way. The tips of the two thumbs come up and just meet over the fingers, lightly. Some teachers say: as if holding a sheet of paper between them. Hands and thumbs make an oval that rests against the belly, near the navel. Here's the clever part. The thumbs are a small gauge. If they press together into a peak, there's probably tension somewhere: effort, trying too hard. If they sag apart into a valley, the mind may be getting dull or drowsy. So some teachers say: don't stare at the mind, check the thumbs. They show the strain before it's noticed anywhere else. With the hands joined and resting, the arms can drop from the shoulders, and the fidgeting has nowhere to go. The hands aren't asleep. They hold a shape that takes almost no effort and just a little attention. Some statues of the Buddha seated in meditation show a resting gesture like this one, a way of saying with the body: nothing to grab right now, nothing to push away.
screen: `ONE HAND RESTING IN THE OTHER.` · `THUMBS JUST TOUCHING.` · `THE THUMBS ARE A GAUGE.` · `NOTHING TO GRAB.` · then, large: `AN OVAL AT THE NAVEL.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and relaxed, lay one hand in the other, left resting on right, and bring the thumb tips up until they just touch, the oval resting near your belly. Keep a little attention in the thumbs: if they press, soften; if they drift apart, gently bring them back. That's the whole job.
The hands. In zazen, the cosmic mudra: one hand resting in the other, thumbs lightly touching, an oval near the navel. Today's word.
Your line: thumbs just touching. A small shape, and a quiet gauge. See you tomorrow.

1209.title: The eyes
1209.hook: eyes half open, gaze resting on the floor ahead
1209.howItsDone: In Zen halls, people commonly sit with eyes half open and gaze lowered; in Soto Zen they often sit facing a wall, and in Rinzai Zen facing into the room.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hands: one resting in the other, an oval near the navel, the thumbs as a gauge. Your line: thumbs just touching.

A cat lies on a sunny windowsill, eyes narrowed to slits. Asleep? Drop a spoon in the kitchen and the ears turn instantly. Not asleep. Not exactly watching, either. Resting, and still there. Ask people what meditation looks like and they'll often shut their eyes to show you. Zen asks for something else: the eyes partly open, lids lowered, gaze on the floor ahead. A little like that cat.
screen: `A CAT WITH EYES IN SLITS.` → `NOT ASLEEP, NOT WATCHING.` → `ZEN KEEPS THE EYES OPEN.`

segments.voice: In zazen the eyes are neither shut nor wide. The lids come halfway down, and the gaze rests on the floor a little way ahead, or on the wall if you're facing one. It isn't fixed on a spot. It's soft, the way eyes rest when someone is listening hard to music. Dogen's guide to sitting is plain about it: keep the eyes open. Why not closed? Two things tend to happen. Drowsiness creeps in, the body taking the hint that it's bedtime. Or a private movie starts: plans, memories, imaginary arguments, and the mind wanders off into its own theater. Half open keeps a little daylight in. Why not wide? Wide eyes grab. They pick out a crack in the paint, a speck on the floor, the person shifting next to you, and attention follows each one. Lowering the lids takes the grip out of looking. Things are still seen; they just aren't chased. Half open is the same pair as the rest of this week. Straight and relaxed in the back. Thumbs just touching in the hands. Here, in the eyes: present to the room, not hunting through it. The world isn't shut out, and it isn't grabbed. Half-open eyes keep the sitter in the room, at rest.
screen: `LIDS HALF DOWN, GAZE ON THE FLOOR.` · `CLOSED: DROWSY OR DREAMING.` · `WIDE: GRABBING AT EVERYTHING.` · `HALF OPEN: IN THE ROOM, AT REST.` · then, large: `SEEN, NOT CHASED.`

segments.voice: In your posture, hands resting, let the eyelids come halfway down and the gaze drop softly to the floor a little way ahead, not fixed on any spot. If the eyes start to close, lift the lids a little; if they start to hunt around, let them settle back. Shapes and light can stay at the edges, and nothing needs looking at.
The eyes. In zazen, half open, lids lowered, the gaze resting softly on the floor ahead: neither shut out nor grabbing. Today's word.

1210.title: Counting breaths
1210.hook: counting out-breaths to ten, the first practice many Zen students learn
1210.howItsDone: In Zen centers, beginners are often taught to count out-breaths from one to ten, returning to one whenever they lose count, before moving to following the breath or to just sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eyes: lids lowered, gaze soft on the floor ahead, like a cat on a windowsill. Your line: half open.

Seven. Eight. Nine. And somewhere around there, the shopping list arrives. Then an email that needs answering. Then a scene from last night's show. Then, with a small jolt: wait, what number was I on? Fourteen? Twenty-two? It can look like failing at a very simple task. Zen sees it differently: that jolt is where the practice actually happens. The posture is built. Now, the breath. Today's word: susokukan.
screen: `SEVEN. EIGHT. NINE.` → `WAIT, WHAT NUMBER WAS I ON?` → `NOW, THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Susokukan is Japanese for the contemplation of counting breaths. In Zen it's often given to beginners early on, sometimes on the first day. The method: sit in this week's posture and let the breath come and go by itself; nothing about it needs to change. On the first out-breath, count one, silently. On the next, two. Up to ten, then start again at one. That's all. Some teachers have students count both the in-breath and the out-breath at first, and only the out-breath later. Then the rule that matters. When the count is lost, or you notice you've sailed past ten, you go back to one. No scolding, no starting the sit over. Just one. In this practice the return is not a detour from the work; it is the work. Someone who loses count fifty times in a sit hasn't failed fifty times. They've come back fifty times. Counting the breath is older than Zen. Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, a classic manual of the Theravada tradition, describes counting as a first step in mindfulness of breathing, a way to tie a wandering mind to something simple. And it is meant to be put down. When the count steadies, teachers may have students drop it and follow the breath without numbers, and later sit with no method at all. Tomorrow, that last step.
screen: `SUSOKUKAN: COUNTING BREATHS.` · `ONE TO TEN, ON THE OUT-BREATH.` · `LOST COUNT? BACK TO ONE.` · `A FIRST STEP, MEANT TO BE PUT DOWN.` · then, large: `THE RETURN IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: In your posture, with the breath going at its own pace, count one silently on the next out-breath, two on the next, up to ten, then begin again at one. When a thought carries you off and you notice, don't argue with it; just come back to one. Reaching ten is fine, and never getting past three is fine too.
Susokukan. Japanese for counting breaths: one to ten on the out-breath, and back to one whenever the count is lost. Today's word.

1211.title: Just sitting, again
1211.hook: sitting with no object at all, as Dogen taught
1211.howItsDone: In Soto Zen, which looks back to Dogen, shikantaza is a central form of zazen, sat in silence facing a wall, often in periods marked by a bell.

segments.voice: Yesterday, susokukan: counting out-breaths, one to ten, and back to one whenever the count slips. Your line: one to ten.

In a monastery hall in China, rows of monks sit in silence. One of them is nodding. His head drops, jerks up, drops again. The abbot, a teacher named Rujing, comes down the row and stops in front of him. Near the sleeper sits a visitor from Japan, Dogen. What the abbot says next, the old accounts tell us, turned Dogen's life. This path met Dogen's just sitting once before, a long way back. Today, again: shikantaza.
screen: `A MONK NODDING OFF.` → `THE ABBOT STOPS.` → `DOGEN IS LISTENING.`

segments.voice: In the story, Rujing tells the dozing monk, in substance: sitting is dropping off body and mind. Why are you sleeping? Sleep is one way of escaping the sitting. Rujing's words point to another way of meeting it: not leaving, not dozing, and not holding on either. Dropping off. The accounts of Dogen's life say that at those words something opened for him. He went to Rujing's room and said that body and mind had dropped off. Rujing confirmed it, and then added, so the story goes, that the dropping off itself should be dropped off. Nothing to hold onto, not even the breakthrough. What Dogen brought home was shikantaza, just sitting: no counting, no question, no image, no goal set out in front. Sitting with no object at all. It sounds easy, and it can be very hard, because there's nothing to do and nowhere to hide. Now look at the week. The sutras went back on the shelf. Then the meditation school. The base and the straight back. The hands. The eyes. The count. Each was a support, and each is still there in shikantaza: the posture stays, the thumbs still touch, the eyes still rest half open. What drops away is the last tool, the count. Only sitting is left: this breath, this room, this body. Just this.
screen: `WHY ARE YOU SLEEPING?` · `BODY AND MIND DROPPED OFF.` · `NO COUNT, NO QUESTION, NO GOAL.` · `THE WEEK'S PIECES, AND THEN NONE.` · then, large: `DROPPING OFF BODY AND MIND.`

segments.voice: Take the week's posture, a stable base, back straight and relaxed, hands in the oval, eyes half open, and count a few breaths if you need to land. Then let the counting go, and don't replace it with anything. When a thought comes, it comes; when it goes, it goes; don't follow it, don't fight it, just sit.
Shikantaza. Japanese for just sitting, nothing but sitting: Dogen's way of zazen, with no object at all. Today's word.
Your line: just this. A whole week of sitting, down to two words. A week on the cushion, done.
